outputs.L4:
The work establishes a relative homotopy principle for smooth maps whose singularities are restricted to a prescribed \(\mathcal K\)-invariant class satisfying suitable mild hypotheses. Here, \(\mathcal K\)-invariance means that the admissible singularity types are unchanged under the natural contact-equivalence action on map germs. The relative form of the principle allows a map, or the relevant differential data, to remain fixed on a specified subset while being deformed elsewhere. Consequently, under the stated assumptions, formal solutions with admissible singularities can be realized—up to homotopy and relative to the fixed region—by genuine smooth maps. This extends the flexibility methods of singularity theory beyond unrestricted mapping problems and provides a systematic way to compare geometric families of singular maps with their formal counterparts.

The work also applies these ideas to the homotopy self-equivalence group of a manifold \(P\). By controlling the singularities that occur in representatives and organizing them according to their nonnegative \(\mathcal K\)-codimension, it constructs a natural filtration of this group. Each stage records those homotopy self-equivalences that can be represented using singularities of bounded complexity, while passage to higher stages permits increasingly complicated singular behavior. The resulting filtration translates geometric information about singular maps into algebraic information about the structure of the self-equivalence group. It therefore offers a framework for identifying successive layers, comparing their invariants, and studying how singularity-theoretic complexity reflects composition and other group-theoretic features of homotopy self-equivalences of \(P\).

This filtration relates singularity-theoretic data to the homotopy structure of mapping spaces and yields a systematic framework for comparing successive stages.

counterfactuals.output:
We study spaces of smooth maps whose singular germs belong to a prescribed collection \(\mathcal S\). We impose the mild hypothesis that every germ in \(\mathcal S\) is finitely \({\cal K}\)-determined and that the resulting \({\cal K}\)-orbit stratification is locally finite. The invariant
\[
\kappa(\sigma)=\operatorname{codim}_{\cal K}(\sigma)
\]
then induces an increasing filtration
\[
\mathcal S_{\le 0}\subseteq \mathcal S_{\le 1}\subseteq\cdots,
\qquad
\mathcal S_{\le r}=\{\sigma\in\mathcal S:\kappa(\sigma)\le r\}.
\]
Passing to the associated classifying spaces, or equivalently to the corresponding Thom spectra, yields a filtration whose successive layers are governed by the normal data of the \({\cal K}\)-strata of codimension \(r\). The resulting spectral sequence organizes the obstruction theory for eliminating higher-codimension singularities and relates the stable topology of mapping spaces to characteristic classes of singular loci.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
